sets.passage:
Magnetic navigation in birds

Every autumn, many songbirds fly thousands of kilometers to warmer regions, often at night and over unfamiliar land. For decades, scientists wondered how such small animals could hold a course with so few visible landmarks. One important answer appears to be the Earth's magnetic field.

In laboratory studies, researchers placed migrating birds in round cages surrounded by electric coils. When the coils were switched on, they shifted the direction of the magnetic field. The birds responded by hopping toward a new side of the cage, as if they were trying to fly in a different direction. This suggested that the birds were sensing magnetic north.

How they sense it is still debated. One theory points to special proteins in the eye that react to magnetism when struck by light. If this is correct, birds might literally see the magnetic field as a faint pattern across their view. Notably, the birds' magnetic sense seems to work poorly in complete darkness, which supports this idea. Most researchers now believe that birds combine this sense with the positions of the stars and the sun.

questions.q: What is the passage mainly about?
choices: Why songbirds migrate at night rather than during the day
How migrating birds may use the Earth's magnetic field to find their way
Why birds become confused by unfamiliar landmarks
How electric coils are used to protect birds during migration
questions.why: 第1段落末で答え（地磁気）を出し、実験と仕組みの説で展開している。

questions.q: According to paragraph 2, what did the birds do when the coils were switched on?
choices: They tried to escape from the top of the cage.
They stopped moving completely.
They moved toward a different part of the cage.
They began to sing more loudly.
questions.why: 第2段落：hopping toward a new side of the cage。

questions.q: The word "faint" in the passage is closest in meaning to
choices: weak
moving
colorful
sharp
questions.why: faint pattern＝かすかな模様。weak が最も近い。

questions.q: Why does the author mention that the magnetic sense works poorly in complete darkness?
choices: To show that birds cannot migrate at night
To argue that stars are more important than magnetism
To explain why the laboratory studies failed
To support the idea that light is involved in sensing magnetism
questions.why: 光で反応するタンパク質説の直後に which supports this idea とある。

questions.q: What can be inferred about bird navigation from the final sentence?
choices: The magnetic sense is useless without the sun.
Birds probably rely on more than one source of information.
Scientists have stopped studying the magnetic sense.
Stars are visible to birds only in autumn.
questions.why: combine this sense with the stars and the sun＝複数の手がかりを使う。

sets.passage:
Reading rock layers

Cliffs and canyon walls often show bands of rock stacked on top of one another. These layers, called strata, form when sediment such as sand, mud, or shells settles in water and is slowly pressed into stone. Because new sediment is laid down on top of older material, geologists generally assume that lower layers are older than the ones above them. This simple rule allows them to place events in order even without knowing exact dates.

The record is rarely perfect, however. In some places, a layer is missing because rivers or wind removed it before the next layer formed. These gaps, known as unconformities, can represent millions of years. In mountain regions, powerful forces in the crust may even fold rock layers so sharply that older strata end up above younger ones.

To deal with such problems, geologists compare layers across wide areas. A distinctive layer, such as one containing a particular fossil or a thin band of volcanic ash, can serve as a marker. If the same marker appears in two distant cliffs, the rocks around it are probably of similar age.

questions.q: According to the passage, why are lower strata usually older?
choices: Newer sediment settles on top of older sediment.
Older rock is heavier and sinks.
Lower layers contain more shells.
Water pressure is greater near the bottom.
questions.why: 第1段落：new sediment is laid down on top of older material。

questions.q: The word "distinctive" in the passage is closest in meaning to
choices: extremely thin
commonly found
very old
easy to recognize
questions.why: distinctive＝はっきり区別できる。marker として使えるのは見分けやすいから。

questions.q: Which of the following is NOT mentioned as a reason the rock record can be incomplete or confusing?
choices: Rivers removing a layer
Wind removing a layer
Sediment hardening too slowly
Layers being folded in mountains
questions.why: 第2段落は川・風による除去と褶曲を挙げる。固まる速さは書かれていない。

questions.q: What is the purpose of paragraph 3?
choices: To explain a method geologists use to overcome problems in the record
To argue that fossils are more useful than dates
To give an example of an unconformity
To describe how volcanic ash is formed
questions.why: 第3段落冒頭：To deal with such problems＝前段の問題への対処法。

questions.q: What can be inferred about two cliffs that both contain the same thin ash layer?
choices: Their lower layers are missing.
They were once part of the same mountain.
Their rocks near that layer likely formed at about the same time.
They contain no fossils.
questions.why: 最終文：the rocks around it are probably of similar age。

sets.passage:
Roman concrete

Many structures built by the ancient Romans are still standing after nearly two thousand years, including harbor walls that have been beaten by seawater for centuries. Modern concrete, by contrast, often begins to crack within a few decades. This difference has led engineers to take a closer look at the Roman recipe.

Roman builders mixed lime with volcanic ash and pieces of rock. When seawater seeped into marine structures made with this mixture, it reacted with the ash to form new minerals inside the concrete. Rather than weakening the material, these minerals filled small cracks and made it stronger over time.

Researchers have also found small white lumps of lime scattered throughout Roman concrete. These were once dismissed as a sign of careless mixing. More recent studies, however, suggest that the lumps were useful: when water entered a crack, it dissolved some of the lime, which then hardened again and sealed the gap. Engineers are now testing whether similar self-healing ingredients could extend the life of modern buildings, although Roman concrete is weaker than modern concrete when first poured.

questions.q: What is the main idea of the passage?
choices: Roman builders were careless when mixing materials.
Seawater is the main cause of damage to buildings.
Modern concrete is stronger than Roman concrete in every way.
Features of Roman concrete may explain why it lasts so long.
questions.why: 長持ちする理由（海水との反応・石灰の塊）を説明する文章。

questions.q: According to paragraph 2, what happened when seawater entered Roman marine structures?
choices: The volcanic ash washed away.
New minerals formed and strengthened the concrete.
The lime turned into sand.
Large cracks quickly appeared.
questions.why: 第2段落：form new minerals … made it stronger over time。

questions.q: The word "dismissed" in the passage is closest in meaning to
choices: quickly removed
widely praised
carefully measured
rejected as unimportant
questions.why: were once dismissed as a sign of careless mixing＝取るに足らない物として退けられた。

questions.q: How did the lime lumps help the concrete, according to recent studies?
choices: They stopped water from entering the concrete.
They dissolved in water and then hardened to seal cracks.
They reacted with sunlight to change color.
They made the concrete lighter.
questions.why: 第3段落：dissolved some of the lime, which then hardened again and sealed the gap。

questions.q: What does the author suggest about Roman concrete in the last sentence?
choices: It was used only for harbor walls.
It cannot be studied in laboratories.
It has a weakness as well as advantages.
It should replace modern concrete immediately.
questions.why: although … weaker than modern concrete when first poured＝利点だけでなく弱点もある。

sets.passage:
Pigments in cave art

Some of the oldest known paintings were made on the walls of caves tens of thousands of years ago. Their images of horses, deer, and handprints are mostly red, yellow, brown, and black. These limited colors reflect the materials that early artists could find.

The reds and yellows came mainly from ochre, a type of earth rich in iron. By heating yellow ochre in a fire, painters could turn it red, which gave them a wider range of shades. Black usually came from charcoal or from minerals containing manganese. The colored powders were mixed with water, animal fat, or plant juices so they would stick to the rock.

Analysis of these pigments has become a valuable tool for archaeologists. Charcoal contains carbon, which can be dated, so black lines can reveal when a painting was made. In some caves, chemical tests have shown that the ochre came from sources many kilometers away. This suggests that the artists either traveled long distances or traded with other groups, a sign that their communities were more connected than once believed.

questions.q: According to paragraph 1, why were the colors in cave paintings limited?
choices: Artists could use only the materials available to them.
The cave walls could not hold other colors.
Bright colors were considered dangerous.
Animals were seen only in a few colors.
questions.why: 第1段落最終文：reflect the materials that early artists could find。

questions.q: What does the passage say about heating yellow ochre?
choices: It made the ochre stick to rock.
It removed the iron from the ochre.
It turned the ochre into charcoal.
It changed the ochre to red.
questions.why: 第2段落：By heating yellow ochre … could turn it red。

questions.q: Why does the author mention that charcoal contains carbon?
choices: To show why black was the most popular color
To describe how charcoal was made
To explain how black lines can help date a painting
To compare charcoal with manganese
questions.why: carbon, which can be dated → 絵の年代が分かる、という流れ。

questions.q: The word "reveal" in the passage is closest in meaning to
choices: hide
show
change
protect
questions.why: reveal when a painting was made＝いつ描かれたかを明らかにする。

questions.q: What can be inferred from the fact that some ochre came from distant sources?
choices: Early communities had more contact with each other than once thought.
Caves were used only by traveling groups.
Local ochre was of poor quality.
Ochre was more valuable than charcoal.
questions.why: 最終文：communities were more connected than once believed。

sets.passage:
Cognitive dissonance

People generally want their beliefs and actions to fit together. When they notice a conflict between the two, they often feel uncomfortable. Psychologists call this feeling cognitive dissonance, and they have found that people work hard to reduce it.

In a well-known type of experiment, participants complete a boring task and are then asked to tell the next participant that it was enjoyable. Some are paid a large amount for saying this, while others receive only a small amount. Later, when asked how much they actually liked the task, those who were paid very little tend to rate it more positively. The researchers' explanation is that well-paid participants could justify their statement by the money. Poorly paid participants had no such excuse, so they reduced their discomfort by changing their opinion of the task.

Dissonance can affect many everyday decisions. After buying an expensive product, for example, shoppers often pay more attention to positive reviews and ignore negative ones. By focusing on information that supports their choice, they protect themselves from the feeling that they may have made a mistake.

questions.q: According to paragraph 1, what is cognitive dissonance?
choices: A preference for agreeing with others
A habit of changing beliefs very often
Discomfort caused by a conflict between beliefs and actions
The ability to complete boring tasks
questions.why: 第1段落：conflict between the two … feel uncomfortable＝cognitive dissonance。

questions.q: In the experiment, which participants rated the task most positively?
choices: Those who received a large payment
Those who did not tell anyone about it
Those who found the task interesting at first
Those who received a small payment
questions.why: those who were paid very little tend to rate it more positively。

questions.q: The word "justify" in the passage is closest in meaning to
choices: give a reason for
hide
apologize for
repeat
questions.why: justify their statement by the money＝お金を理由に説明がつく。

questions.q: Why does the author mention shoppers who buy expensive products?
choices: To explain why reviews are often negative
To give an everyday example of reducing dissonance
To show that expensive products are better
To describe a second laboratory experiment
questions.why: 第3段落：Dissonance can affect many everyday decisions → For example。

questions.q: Based on the passage, which of the following would a person feeling dissonance most likely do?
choices: Tell others about a mistake immediately
Avoid making any decisions
Change an opinion so it matches an action already taken
Ask for more money before doing a task
questions.why: 実験の低報酬グループは意見を変えて不快感を減らした。

sets.passage:
Urban heat islands

On summer evenings, the center of a large city can be several degrees warmer than the surrounding countryside. This pattern is known as the urban heat island effect. It occurs mainly because city surfaces such as asphalt, concrete, and dark roofs absorb a great deal of sunlight during the day and release the heat slowly after sunset.

Other factors add to the problem. Cities have fewer trees and less open soil, so less water evaporates to cool the air. Tall buildings can block wind that would otherwise carry heat away. Cars, air conditioners, and factories also give off heat directly.

The effect is more than a matter of comfort. Higher night temperatures can make heat waves more dangerous, especially for older people, and they increase the demand for electricity. As a result, many cities are experimenting with solutions. Painting roofs white or light gray reflects sunlight instead of absorbing it. Planting street trees provides shade, and parks with grass and ponds help cool nearby neighborhoods. Some cities have even replaced parking lots with surfaces that allow rainwater to soak into the ground.

questions.q: According to paragraph 1, what is the main cause of the urban heat island effect?
choices: Cities receive more sunlight than the countryside.
City surfaces store heat during the day and release it at night.
Wind brings warm air from rural areas.
Rain rarely falls in large cities.
questions.why: 第1段落最終文：absorb … sunlight during the day and release the heat slowly after sunset。

questions.q: Which of the following is NOT mentioned as a factor that adds to city heat?
choices: Large numbers of people walking outdoors
Heat from cars and air conditioners
Buildings that block wind
A lack of trees
questions.why: 第2段落は木の少なさ・風を遮るビル・車やエアコンの熱。歩行者は出てこない。

questions.q: The phrase "give off" in the passage is closest in meaning to
choices: repair
require
reduce
release
questions.why: give off heat＝熱を出す。

questions.q: Why does the author mention older people?
choices: To explain who uses the most electricity
To show that the effect can harm health
To describe who lives in city centers
To argue that parks should be built for them
questions.why: The effect is more than a matter of comfort → 熱波で危険＝健康への害。

questions.q: What do the solutions in paragraph 3 have in common?
choices: They reduce the amount of heat that city areas hold.
They require replacing tall buildings.
They make cities warmer in winter.
They are all paid for by electricity companies.
questions.why: 白い屋根・街路樹・公園・水が染み込む舗装は、どれも街にたまる熱を減らす。

sets.passage:
Life at deep-sea vents

For a long time, scientists assumed that almost all life on Earth depended on energy from the sun. Plants capture sunlight, and animals eat plants or other animals. That assumption was challenged when explorers discovered communities of animals living around hot springs on the dark ocean floor.

These hot springs, called hydrothermal vents, release water heated by volcanic activity beneath the seabed. The water is rich in dissolved chemicals such as hydrogen sulfide, which is poisonous to most animals. Yet certain bacteria can use these chemicals to make food, a process called chemosynthesis. The bacteria form the base of a food web that includes giant tube worms, clams, shrimp, and crabs.

Some vent animals have formed remarkable partnerships with the bacteria. Adult giant tube worms have no mouth or stomach. Instead, they carry bacteria inside their bodies and supply them with chemicals from the water, and the bacteria in turn provide the worms with nutrients. Discoveries like these have encouraged scientists to consider whether life might exist in similar dark environments elsewhere, such as the oceans thought to lie beneath the ice of some moons.

questions.q: What assumption was challenged by the discovery of vent communities?
choices: That bacteria are always harmful
That animals cannot live in cold water
That volcanoes exist only on land
That nearly all life depends on sunlight
questions.why: 第1段落：almost all life … depended on energy from the sun という前提が覆された。

questions.q: According to paragraph 2, how do bacteria at the vents make food?
choices: By capturing faint sunlight
By absorbing heat from the rocks
By using chemicals in the vent water
By eating small shrimp
questions.why: certain bacteria can use these chemicals to make food（化学合成）。

questions.q: The word "remarkable" in the passage is closest in meaning to
choices: simple
temporary
unusual and impressive
dangerous
questions.why: remarkable partnerships＝驚くべき共生関係。

questions.q: What is stated about adult giant tube worms?
choices: They leave the vents to find food.
They produce hydrogen sulfide.
They eat clams and shrimp.
They depend on bacteria living inside them for nutrients.
questions.why: 口も胃も無く、体内の細菌から栄養をもらう。

questions.q: Why does the author mention moons with oceans beneath their ice?
choices: To suggest places where life might exist without sunlight
To compare the temperature of different oceans
To show that tube worms live in space
To explain where hydrothermal vents came from
questions.why: 最終文：life might exist in similar dark environments elsewhere。

sets.passage:
Perspective in Renaissance painting

Before the fifteenth century, many European paintings showed figures and buildings in a way that looked flat. Important people were often painted larger than others, regardless of where they stood in the scene. During the Renaissance, however, artists in Italy developed a system called linear perspective that made flat surfaces appear to have depth.

The key idea of linear perspective is the vanishing point. Lines that are parallel in real life, such as the edges of a road or the rows of tiles on a floor, are drawn so that they meet at a single point on the horizon. Objects are also made smaller as they move farther from the viewer. Together, these rules create a convincing sense of distance.

The new method spread quickly, partly because it was closely linked to mathematics and could be taught step by step. Artists' guidebooks explained how to construct a scene with rulers and measured lines. Perspective changed not only painting but also architecture and stage design, and it remained the standard way of representing space in Western art for several centuries.

questions.q: According to paragraph 1, how were important people often shown before the fifteenth century?
choices: Standing on the horizon
Larger than other figures
In darker colors
Farther away from the viewer
questions.why: 第1段落：Important people were often painted larger than others。

questions.q: Which of the following best describes a vanishing point?
choices: The largest object in a painting
A point where the artist signs the work
The place where lines that are parallel in reality appear to meet
The edge of the painting where objects disappear
questions.why: 第2段落：parallel lines are drawn so that they meet at a single point on the horizon。

questions.q: The word "convincing" in the passage is closest in meaning to
choices: colorful
temporary
surprising
believable
questions.why: convincing sense of distance＝本物らしく感じられる奥行き。

questions.q: According to paragraph 3, why did linear perspective spread quickly?
choices: It was cheaper than older methods.
It could be learned through clear, mathematical steps.
It required no tools at all.
It was demanded by architects.
questions.why: closely linked to mathematics and could be taught step by step。

questions.q: What can be inferred about linear perspective from the final sentence?
choices: Its influence went beyond painting and lasted a long time.
It was soon replaced by flatter styles.
It was difficult for architects to apply.
It was used only in Italy.
questions.why: 建築・舞台にも広がり、数世紀にわたり標準だった。

sets.passage:
Railways and standard time

Until the nineteenth century, most towns kept their own local time. Clocks were set so that noon was the moment the sun stood highest in the sky. Because the sun reaches that point at slightly different moments in different places, a town to the east would be a few minutes ahead of a town to the west.

These small differences caused few problems when travel was slow. The spread of railways changed that. A train might pass through dozens of towns, each with its own time, and printed timetables became extremely confusing. Some stations displayed several clocks at once, one for each railway company that used them.

To solve the problem, railway companies began to adopt standard time, in which every place within a large region used the same clock time. The idea met some resistance at first, as people were used to following the sun. Over time, however, governments made standard time official, and the world was eventually divided into time zones. The change shows how a new technology can reshape something as basic as the way people measure the day.

questions.q: Why did towns once keep different times?
choices: Governments required each town to choose a time.
Clocks in the past were not accurate.
Railway companies set the time in each town.
Each town set noon by the position of the sun.
questions.why: 第1段落：noon was the moment the sun stood highest。場所ごとに違う。

questions.q: According to paragraph 2, why did local time become a problem?
choices: Towns refused to share their clocks.
Trains could not run at night.
Railways made timetables across many towns confusing.
The sun's position became harder to measure.
questions.why: 鉄道が多くの町を通るので timetables became extremely confusing。

questions.q: Why does the author mention stations with several clocks?
choices: To describe a popular decoration
To illustrate how confusing time had become
To show that stations were well equipped
To explain how standard time was measured
questions.why: 混乱ぶりの具体例として挙げている。

questions.q: The word "resistance" in the passage is closest in meaning to
choices: opposition
support
delay
confusion
questions.why: met some resistance＝反対にあった。

questions.q: What is the author's main point in the final sentence?
choices: Railways are the most important invention in history.
People should return to following the sun.
Technology can change even basic parts of daily life.
Time zones are still controversial today.
questions.why: a new technology can reshape something as basic as … measure the day。

sets.passage:
Default options

Traditional economic theory assumes that people make choices by carefully weighing costs and benefits. Behavioral economists, however, have shown that the way choices are presented can strongly influence what people decide, even when the options themselves stay the same.

One powerful example is the default option, which is what happens if a person does nothing. In many workplaces, employees can join a retirement savings plan. When joining requires filling out a form, a large share of workers never sign up. When workers are enrolled automatically and must fill out a form to leave, participation often rises sharply. The plan and its benefits are identical in both cases; only the default has changed.

Several explanations have been offered. Making a decision takes effort, and people tend to put off tasks that are not urgent. Some may also see the default as a recommendation from the employer. Supporters argue that well-designed defaults can help people act in their own long-term interest. Critics reply that defaults may push people toward choices they would not make on reflection, so they should be used openly and with care.

questions.q: What is the passage mainly about?
choices: Why traditional economic theory is always correct
How employers design application forms
Why retirement plans have become more expensive
How the presentation of choices, especially defaults, affects decisions
questions.why: 第1段落で提示の仕方が影響すると述べ、デフォルトの例で展開している。

questions.q: According to paragraph 2, what happens when workers are enrolled automatically?
choices: The benefits of the plan increase.
Many more workers end up in the savings plan.
Fewer workers stay with the company.
Workers must pay a fee to leave the plan.
questions.why: participation often rises sharply。

questions.q: Why does the author state that the plan and its benefits are identical in both cases?
choices: To show that only the default explains the difference
To suggest that employers are dishonest
To explain why forms are necessary
To argue that the plan is not worth joining
questions.why: only the default has changed＝違いの原因はデフォルトだけ。

questions.q: The phrase "put off" in the passage is closest in meaning to
choices: finish
delay
enjoy
refuse
questions.why: put off tasks that are not urgent＝急がない仕事を先延ばしする。

questions.q: What do the critics mentioned in paragraph 3 believe?
choices: Defaults should be used openly because they can steer people's choices.
Defaults have no real effect on behavior.
Workers should never save for retirement.
Forms should be removed from all workplaces.
questions.why: push people toward choices … should be used openly and with care。

parts.title: Listening: Listen to an Academic Talk
parts.desc: 約200語の講義を聞いて4問（主題・詳細・例の目的・推測）
parts.tip: 最初に言う「今日の話題」を必ずつかむ。例（For example / Imagine …）は、直前の主張を説明するために出てくる。But / Now, here's something interesting の後は大事な点。
parts.intro: Listen to part of a talk in a class. Then answer the questions.

sets.script: Today let's look at an animal that lives in two very different worlds: the frog. Most frogs begin life as eggs laid in water. The eggs hatch into tadpoles, which breathe through gills and swim with a tail, a lot like fish. Over a few weeks or months, the tadpole goes through a dramatic change called metamorphosis. It grows legs, its tail is absorbed into its body, and it develops lungs so it can breathe air. Now, here's something interesting. Adult frogs also breathe through their skin. That's why their skin has to stay moist. And it's also why frogs are often called indicator species. Because chemicals in the water and air pass easily through their skin, frogs are very sensitive to pollution. So when frog populations in an area start to decline, scientists take it as an early warning that something may be wrong with the environment.

questions.q: What is the talk mainly about?
choices: The life cycle of frogs and their sensitivity to the environment
How fish and frogs are related

questions.why: 変態の説明から、皮膚呼吸と環境指標の話へ進む。

questions.why: grows legs … develops lungs。尾は吸収される。

sets.script: Last week we talked about how minerals form. Today I want to focus on one way geologists identify them: hardness. In the early nineteenth century, a scale was developed that ranks minerals from one to ten. Talc, which is soft enough to scratch with a fingernail, is a one. Diamond, the hardest natural mineral, is a ten. The test is simple. If mineral A can scratch mineral B, then A is harder. Now, one common misunderstanding is that the scale is evenly spaced. It isn't. The scale only tells you the order. Diamond, at ten, is actually several times harder than corundum, at nine. So the jump from nine to ten is much bigger than the jump from one to two. In the field, geologists often carry simple tools to test hardness — a steel nail, a piece of glass, even a copper coin — because these have known positions on the scale.

questions.q: What is the main topic of the talk?
choices: Why some minerals are more valuable than others
How diamonds are formed
The history of geology in the nineteenth century
A scale used to measure the hardness of minerals
questions.why: Today I want to focus on … hardness。

choices: They weigh both minerals.
They check which one can scratch the other.
They compare their colors.
They heat both minerals.
questions.why: If mineral A can scratch mineral B, then A is harder。

questions.q: What misunderstanding does the professor mention?
choices: That the steps on the scale are equal in size
That talc is harder than diamond
That hardness cannot be tested in the field
That the scale has twelve levels
questions.why: the scale is evenly spaced. It isn't。

questions.q: Why does the professor mention a steel nail and a copper coin?
choices: They can scratch diamond.
They are examples of minerals.
They are simple objects with known hardness used in the field.
They were used to create the scale.
questions.why: these have known positions on the scale。

sets.script: When we think of the Silk Road, we often picture a single road running from China to the Mediterranean. In reality, it was a huge network of routes over land and sea, and very few traders ever traveled the whole distance. Instead, goods were passed from one merchant to the next, often changing hands many times. A bolt of silk might be traded at a market in Central Asia, carried further west by another group, and sold again before reaching its final buyer. Each time, the price went up. And it wasn't just silk. Spices, paper, glass, horses, and precious metals moved along these routes. But perhaps the most important things that traveled weren't goods at all. Ideas did too: religions, languages, farming techniques, and even mathematical knowledge. In that sense, the Silk Road was as much a network of communication as a network of trade.

questions.q: What point does the professor make about the Silk Road?
choices: It was used mainly for sea travel.

It connected only two cities.
It was built by one powerful empire.
questions.why: In reality, it was a huge network of routes。

choices: Taxes were charged only at the final market.
Silk became rarer in the west.
Goods were sold many times by different merchants.
Traders traveled very slowly.
questions.why: changing hands many times … Each time, the price went up。

questions.q: Which of the following is NOT mentioned as something that traveled along the routes?

questions.why: spices, paper, glass, horses, metals, ideas。印刷された本は言っていない。

choices: The exchange of ideas was as significant as the exchange of goods.

questions.why: as much a network of communication as a network of trade。

sets.script: Let's talk about why some colors seem to move or vibrate in a painting, even though the paint is perfectly still. It has to do with something called complementary colors. On a color wheel, complementary colors sit directly opposite each other — red and green, blue and orange, yellow and purple. When you place two complementary colors side by side, each one makes the other look more intense. Painters have used this for centuries, but in the nineteenth and twentieth centuries some artists made it a central part of their work. By putting small dots or strokes of complementary colors next to each other, they created surfaces that seemed to shimmer. There's actually a biological reason for this. When you stare at one color for a while, the cells in your eye that respond to it get tired, and you start to see its complement. Artists didn't always know the science, but they understood the effect from experience.

questions.q: What is the talk mainly about?
choices: How to mix paint on a color wheel

How complementary colors create strong visual effects
The history of a single famous painting
questions.why: complementary colors が強い効果を生む理由の講義。

questions.q: What happens when complementary colors are placed next to each other?
choices: Each color appears more intense.
The colors seem to blend into one.
Both colors appear gray.
The colors look darker.
questions.why: each one makes the other look more intense。

questions.q: What biological explanation does the professor give?
choices: Bright light damages the eye.
Eye cells that respond to a color become tired.
The brain cannot see two colors at once.
Some people cannot see green.
questions.why: the cells in your eye that respond to it get tired。

questions.q: What does the professor imply about the artists?
choices: They studied biology before painting.
They avoided using complementary colors.
They invented the color wheel.
They learned about the effect through practice rather than science.
questions.why: didn't always know the science, but understood the effect from experience。

sets.script: Have you ever noticed that you remember unfinished tasks better than finished ones? This idea goes back to early research in psychology. A researcher noticed that waiters could remember complex orders perfectly — until the bill was paid. After that, they forgot the details almost immediately. To test this, experiments were designed in which people were given a series of simple tasks, like puzzles, and were interrupted before finishing some of them. Later, when asked to recall the tasks, participants remembered the interrupted ones about twice as often. This became known as the Zeigarnik effect, after the researcher. Now, later studies have shown that the effect isn't always strong; it depends on things like how motivated people are to finish. But it does suggest a practical study tip. If you stop studying in the middle of a section rather than at the end, you may find it easier to pick up where you left off.

questions.q: What observation led to the early research?
choices: People could not finish simple tasks.
Waiters forgot orders once the customers had paid.
Students remembered puzzles better than words.
Customers often forgot what they ordered.
questions.why: waiters … remember orders perfectly — until the bill was paid。

questions.q: What did the experiments find?
choices: Interrupted tasks were remembered more often.
Finished tasks were remembered twice as often.
Interruptions made people angry.
Puzzles were harder than other tasks.
questions.why: remembered the interrupted ones about twice as often。

questions.q: What does the professor say about later studies?
choices: They showed the effect is stronger in waiters.
They proved the effect does not exist.
They used only puzzles.
They found the effect depends on factors such as motivation.
questions.why: isn't always strong; it depends on … how motivated people are。

questions.q: Why does the professor mention stopping in the middle of a section?
choices: To criticize students who study too long
To show that interruptions are harmful
To give a practical application of the effect
To explain how the experiments were designed
questions.why: it does suggest a practical study tip。

sets.script: Today's topic is something economists call the tragedy of the commons. Imagine a village pasture that anyone can use to feed their cows. For each farmer, adding one more cow is a good deal: the farmer gets all the benefit of the extra milk, while the cost — a little less grass — is shared by everyone. The problem is that every farmer thinks the same way. So more and more cows are added until the grass is gone, and everyone loses. The same pattern appears with fishing in open waters, with groundwater, and even with traffic on a free road. Now, for a long time, people assumed the only solutions were government rules or private ownership. But research on real communities found a third option. Many groups have managed shared resources successfully for generations by setting their own rules — limiting how much each member can take and watching each other to make sure the rules are followed.

questions.q: What is the main idea of the tragedy of the commons?
choices: Milk prices rise when grass is scarce.
Governments always manage land poorly.
Individuals acting in their own interest can destroy a shared resource.
Villages should not allow farmers to own cows.
questions.why: 各自が得をしようとして、全員が損をする。

questions.q: Why does each farmer want to add another cow?
choices: The farmer gains the full benefit but shares the cost.
Cows eat less grass in large groups.
The pasture is owned by the farmer.
The government pays for each cow.
questions.why: gets all the benefit … the cost is shared by everyone。

questions.q: Why does the professor mention fishing and traffic?
choices: To explain how roads are built
To argue that fishing should be banned
To compare different types of farming
To show that the same problem occurs in other situations
questions.why: The same pattern appears with fishing … traffic。

questions.q: What third option does the professor describe?
choices: Selling the pasture to one farmer
Communities creating and enforcing their own rules
Removing all cows from the pasture
Asking a government to set prices
questions.why: groups … setting their own rules … watching each other。

sets.script: Most people think of deserts as places where nothing grows. But many plants have adapted to survive there. Let's look at three strategies. First, some plants store water. Cactuses, for example, have thick stems that can swell after rain and shrink during long dry periods. Second, some plants reduce water loss. Instead of broad leaves, cactuses have spines, which lose much less water and also protect the plant from animals. Many desert plants also open the tiny holes in their surfaces, called stomata, only at night, when it's cooler and less water evaporates. The third strategy is avoidance. Some desert flowers spend most of their lives as seeds in the soil. When a heavy rain finally comes, they sprout, flower, and produce new seeds within just a few weeks, and then they die. So the desert can suddenly fill with color for a short time after a storm.

questions.q: How does the professor organize the talk?
choices: By describing three survival strategies
By comparing deserts on different continents
By listing plants from smallest to largest
By telling the history of desert research
questions.why: Let's look at three strategies。

questions.q: What is one function of cactus spines mentioned in the talk?
choices: They help the plant grow taller.
They collect rainwater.
They protect the plant from animals.
They attract insects.
questions.why: lose much less water and also protect the plant from animals。

questions.q: Why do many desert plants open their stomata only at night?
choices: They need moonlight to grow.
Animals are less active at night.
The soil is wetter at night.
Less water is lost when it is cooler.
questions.why: when it's cooler and less water evaporates。

questions.q: What can be inferred about the desert flowers described at the end?
choices: They live for many years above ground.
They complete their life cycle very quickly after rain.
They grow only in winter.
They store water in thick stems.
questions.why: 数週間で発芽・開花・種まで終えて枯れる。

sets.script: In the early days of photography, many painters worried that the camera would make them unnecessary. After all, a photograph could record a face or a landscape more accurately than any brush. And in fact, the market for small painted portraits did shrink as photography studios opened. But the effect on art turned out to be more complicated. Freed from the job of simply copying what they saw, some painters began to explore what a camera couldn't do — expressing emotion, playing with color, or showing a scene from several angles at once. At the same time, photography itself influenced painting. Photographs captured moments that the eye usually misses, such as the exact position of a running horse's legs. Some painters studied these images closely and changed the way they showed motion. So rather than replacing painting, photography pushed it in new directions.

questions.q: What did many painters fear when photography appeared?
choices: That photography would be too expensive
That photographs would damage paintings
That studios would stop selling paint
That cameras would replace their work
questions.why: the camera would make them unnecessary。

questions.q: What does the professor say about small painted portraits?
choices: They became more popular.
There was less demand for them.
They were painted only by photographers.
They were copied from photographs.
questions.why: the market for small painted portraits did shrink。

questions.q: Why does the professor mention a running horse?
choices: To explain why painters disliked photography
To describe a famous painting
To illustrate how photographs revealed details people normally miss
To show that horses were difficult to photograph
questions.why: moments that the eye usually misses の例。

questions.q: What is the professor's main conclusion?
choices: Photography encouraged painting to change and develop.
Photography completely replaced painting.
Painters should avoid using photographs.
Painting had no effect on photography.
questions.why: rather than replacing painting, photography pushed it in new directions。

sets.script: Why do bubbles form in markets? A bubble happens when the price of something — houses, stocks, even flowers — rises far above what most experts think it's really worth. One key factor is expectations. If people believe a price will keep rising, they buy, not because they need the item, but because they expect to sell it later for more. That buying pushes the price higher, which seems to confirm their belief, and even more people join in. For a while, this cycle feeds itself. But at some point, buyers start to doubt that prices can go any higher. When enough people try to sell at the same time, prices can fall very quickly. Economists still debate how to identify a bubble before it bursts. The difficulty is that a rising price doesn't always mean a bubble; sometimes the value has genuinely increased.

questions.q: How does the professor define a bubble?
choices: A price far above what most experts believe something is worth
Any price that rises quickly
A sudden fall in the price of flowers
A market where nothing is sold
questions.why: rises far above what most experts think it's really worth。

questions.q: According to the professor, why do people buy during a bubble?
choices: They need the item for daily use.
Prices are lower than usual.
They expect to sell later at a higher price.
The government encourages them.
questions.why: because they expect to sell it later for more。

questions.q: What causes prices to fall quickly?
choices: New buyers entering the market
A shortage of the item
Experts changing their definitions
Many people trying to sell at once
questions.why: When enough people try to sell at the same time。

questions.q: Why is it difficult to identify a bubble in advance?
choices: Bubbles happen only with houses.
A rising price may reflect a real increase in value.
Prices never rise for long.
Economists do not study prices.
questions.why: a rising price doesn't always mean a bubble。

parts.title: Writing: Build a Sentence
parts.desc: 会話の返事を、ばらばらの語句を並べて1文にする（Writing セクション）
parts.tip: まず主語と動詞を見つけて骨組みを作り、残りを後ろにつなぐ。疑問文か、間接疑問（I'm not sure who …）か、時制の一致はどうかを確かめる。全部の語句を1回ずつ使う。
parts.intro: Make an appropriate reply by putting the words and phrases in the correct order. Type the full sentence.

questions.q: “Where did you leave the lab key?”  Reply: ____  [ I / at / the front desk / left it ]
answer: I left it at the front desk
questions.why: 主語＋動詞＋目的語＋場所の順。left it at …。

questions.q: “Do you know when the essay is due?”  Reply: ____  [ Monday / I think / it's due / next ]
answer: I think it's due next Monday
questions.why: I think の後に普通の語順の文（it's due …）。

questions.q: “Why are you taking the bus today?”  Reply: ____  [ has / my bike / a / flat tire ]
answer: my bike has a flat tire
questions.why: 主語 my bike ＋ has a flat tire（パンクしている）。

questions.q: “Can you tell me where the career office is?”  Reply: ____  [ the student center / of / it's / on the second floor ]
answer: it's on the second floor of the student center
questions.why: 場所は on the second floor of … と「階→建物」の順。

questions.q: “What did the professor say about the quiz?”  Reply: ____  [ she said / it / postponed / would be ]
answer: she said it would be postponed
questions.why: 時制の一致：said の後は would be postponed。

questions.q: “Have you finished the reading?”  Reply: ____  [ but / I'll / finish it tonight / not yet ]
answer: not yet but I'll finish it tonight
questions.why: Not yet, but I'll … が自然な返事。

questions.q: “Could you help me move this table?”  Reply: ____  [ to put it / sure / do you want / where ]
answer: sure where do you want to put it
questions.why: Where do you want to put it? 疑問詞＋do you want＋to 不定詞。

questions.q: “Did you enjoy the guest lecture?”  Reply: ____  [ more interesting / it was / yes / than I expected ]
answer: yes it was more interesting than I expected
questions.why: 比較：more interesting than I expected。

questions.q: “I can't open the course website.”  Reply: ____  [ logging in / have you tried / with / your student ID ]
answer: have you tried logging in with your student ID
questions.why: have you tried ＋ -ing（〜してみた？）。

questions.q: “Who is leading tomorrow's discussion?”  Reply: ____  [ who / lead it / I'm not sure / will ]
answer: I'm not sure who will lead it
questions.why: 間接疑問：I'm not sure who will lead it（疑問文の語順にしない）。

questions.q: “Is the library open on Sunday?”  Reply: ____  [ at / noon / on weekends / it opens ]
answer: it opens at noon on weekends
questions.why: 時刻 at noon、曜日のくくり on weekends。

questions.q: “How was your field trip?”  Reply: ____  [ some amazing / saw / we / rock formations ]
answer: we saw some amazing rock formations
questions.why: 主語＋動詞＋形容詞＋名詞。

questions.q: “Why didn't you come to the meeting?”  Reply: ____  [ it had been / I / didn't know / moved to today ]
answer: I didn't know it had been moved to today
questions.why: 過去完了：it had been moved（知らなかった時点より前に変更）。

questions.q: “Should I bring anything to the study group?”  Reply: ____  [ from last week / could you / the notes / bring ]
answer: could you bring the notes from last week
questions.why: Could you bring …? 依頼の形。

questions.q: “What are you doing this summer?”  Reply: ____  [ to get / an internship / I'm hoping / at a museum ]
answer: I'm hoping to get an internship at a museum
questions.why: hope to ＋動詞。I'm hoping to get …。

questions.q: “Did you find a roommate?”  Reply: ____  [ next month / is moving in / yes / a friend of mine ]
answer: yes a friend of mine is moving in next month
questions.why: 現在進行形で近い未来の予定：is moving in next month。

questions.q: “Where can I print my poster?”  Reply: ____  [ up to one meter wide / can print / posters / the copy center ]
answer: the copy center can print posters up to one meter wide
questions.why: 主語 the copy center ＋ can print ＋目的語＋説明。

questions.q: “Are you going to the concert tonight?”  Reply: ____  [ I have / but / I'd like to / an exam tomorrow ]
answer: I'd like to but I have an exam tomorrow
questions.why: I'd like to, but … 断りの定番。

questions.q: “How long have you been studying Spanish?”  Reply: ____  [ I've been / about two years / for / studying it ]
answer: I've been studying it for about two years
questions.why: 現在完了進行形＋for ＋期間。

questions.q: “Can I borrow your calculator?”  Reply: ____  [ of course / after class / just / give it back ]
answer: of course just give it back after class
questions.why: Of course, just give it back after class. 命令文。

questions.q: “Is Dr. Patel's office in this building?”  Reply: ____  [ her office / across / is / the hall ]
answer: her office is across the hall
questions.why: across the hall（廊下の向かい）。

questions.q: “What should I do if I miss the bus?”  Reply: ____  [ call / you / can / a campus taxi ]
answer: you can call a campus taxi
questions.why: 助動詞 can ＋動詞の原形。

questions.q: “Why is the café so crowded?”  Reply: ____  [ free / giving away / coffee today / they're ]
answer: they're giving away free coffee today
questions.why: 現在進行形 they're giving away（無料で配っている）。

questions.q: “Did the experiment work?”  Reply: ____  [ not / what we expected / were / the results ]
answer: the results were not what we expected
questions.why: what we expected＝「私たちが予想したこと」。名詞のかたまり。

questions.q: “Do you know whose jacket this is?”  Reply: ____  [ I / to Ken / it belongs / think ]
answer: I think it belongs to Ken
questions.why: belong to ＋人（〜の物だ）。

questions.q: “When does registration open?”  Reply: ____  [ opens / two weeks / before the semester / it ]
answer: it opens two weeks before the semester
questions.why: 期間＋before ＋名詞。

questions.q: “Have you seen my blue notebook?”  Reply: ____  [ I / in the lounge / saw one / on the table ]
answer: I saw one on the table in the lounge
in the lounge I saw one on the table
questions.why: 目的語の後に場所を「小→大」で並べる。

questions.q: “Could you explain how to use this machine?”  Reply: ____  [ you need / your card / first / to insert ]
answer: first you need to insert your card
you need to insert your card first
questions.why: First, you need to insert … 手順の説明。

questions.q: “Which topic did you choose for your paper?”  Reply: ____  [ local farming / the history of / I'm writing / about ]
answer: I'm writing about the history of local farming
questions.why: write about ＋名詞句。the history of local farming。

questions.q: “Is it OK if I sit here?”  Reply: ____  [ is / sure / nobody / using that seat ]
answer: sure nobody is using that seat
questions.why: Nobody is using that seat. 否定の主語 nobody。

parts.title: Writing: Write an Email
parts.desc: 状況に合わせてメールを書く（7分）
parts.tip: 書き出し（Dear …,）→用件1文→指示された3つの点→結び（Thank you … / Best regards,）。3つの点を全部入れることが一番大事。相手に合わせて丁寧さを変える。
parts.intro: Read the situation and write an email. You have 7 minutes.

sets.prompt:
You are taking an online course in environmental science. The professor has asked each student to visit a local park and write a short report, but the park near you has been closed for repairs for the next month.

Write an email to your professor. In your email:
- explain the problem
- suggest another way to complete the assignment
- ask whether the deadline can be changed
sets.note: 3つの点をすべて書く。丁寧な書き出しと結びを入れる。

sets.prompt:
You recently joined a university hiking club. The club's next trip is on a weekend when you have a family event, but you would still like to take part in the club's activities.

Write an email to the club leader. In your email:
- explain why you cannot go on the next trip
- describe what kind of activities you enjoy
- ask how else you can be involved this month
sets.note: 理由・好み・質問の3つを段落かつなぎ語で分ける。

sets.prompt:
You bought a used textbook from the campus bookstore. When you got home, you found that several pages were missing.

Write an email to the bookstore manager. In your email:
- describe the problem with the book
- explain why you need the book soon
- say what you would like the store to do
sets.note: 苦情でも丁寧に。具体的に（何ページ・いつ必要か）。

sets.prompt:
Your study group has been meeting in a library room every Tuesday evening. This week, the library has told you the room is no longer available on Tuesdays.

Write an email to the members of your study group. In your email:
- explain what has happened
- suggest a new time or place
- ask members to reply with their preference
sets.note: 仲間あてなので少しくだけてよいが、文は正確に。

sets.prompt:
You would like to work as a research assistant for a professor whose class you enjoyed last semester. You have not talked with the professor about this before.

Write an email to the professor. In your email:
- introduce yourself and mention the class you took
- explain why you are interested in the research
- ask whether any positions are available
sets.note: 自己紹介→理由→質問の順。I am writing to … で始めると楽。

sets.prompt:
The air conditioner in your dormitory room has stopped working, and it has been very hot for several days. You reported it once, but nobody has come to fix it.

Write an email to the housing office. In your email:
- describe the problem and how long it has lasted
- explain how it is affecting you
- request a specific action
sets.note: 経過（いつ報告したか）を入れると説得力が出る。

sets.prompt:
A classmate lent you a book for a project, but you accidentally spilled coffee on it and damaged several pages.

Write an email to your classmate. In your email:
- explain what happened
- apologize
- offer a way to make up for the damage
sets.note: 謝罪は具体的に。償いの方法を1つ提案する。

sets.prompt:
You read on the university website that the campus gym is planning to reduce its weekend hours. You use the gym mostly on weekends.

Write an email to the gym director. In your email:
- explain how you use the gym
- describe how the change would affect you and other students
- suggest an alternative
sets.note: 反対意見＋代案。感情ではなく理由で。

parts.title: Writing: Write for an Academic Discussion
parts.desc: 教授の問いと学生2人の投稿を読み、自分の意見を書く（10分・100語以上）
parts.tip: 1文目で自分の立場をはっきり書く。他の学生の意見に一言触れ、2人が言っていない理由か具体例を足す。最後に短くまとめる。
parts.intro: Read the professor's question and the two student posts. Write a post that adds your own opinion to the discussion. You have 10 minutes.

sets.prompt:
Your professor is teaching a class on psychology. Write a post responding to the professor's question.

Professor: Many students study while listening to music. Some researchers say music helps people stay focused, while others say it divides attention. In your experience, does listening to music while studying help or hurt learning? Why?

Maya: Music helps me a lot. When I study in silence, I get bored and start checking my phone. Calm music without words keeps me at my desk longer.

Tom: I think it depends on the task. Music is fine for simple work like organizing notes, but when I read difficult material, any sound distracts me.
sets.note: 自分の立場を最初に。2人の意見に一言触れ、新しい理由か例を足す。

sets.prompt:
Your professor is teaching a class on economics. Write a post responding to the professor's question.

Professor: Some cities charge drivers a fee to enter the city center during busy hours. Supporters say it reduces traffic and pollution; critics say it is unfair to people with lower incomes. Do you think such fees are a good policy? Why or why not?

Lena: I support the fees. Traffic in city centers wastes time and damages health. If driving costs more, people will choose buses and trains.

Omar: I disagree. Workers who live far away may have no good public transport. A fee would punish people who have no choice.
sets.note: Lena と Omar のどちらに近いかを示し、2人が言っていない理由を1つ。

sets.prompt:
Your professor is teaching a class on history. Write a post responding to the professor's question.

Professor: When we study history, we can focus on famous leaders and major events, or on the daily lives of ordinary people. Which approach do you think helps students understand the past better? Why?

Kenji: Leaders and major events shaped everything else. Without understanding them, the daily lives of ordinary people do not make sense.

Sara: I prefer learning about ordinary people. Most people in history were farmers and workers, and their lives tell us what the past was really like.
sets.note: どちらか一方を選ぶか、両方の良さを言ってから自分の重みづけを示す。

sets.prompt:
Your professor is teaching a class on biology. Write a post responding to the professor's question.

Professor: Zoos spend large amounts of money to protect endangered animals through breeding programs. Some people believe that money would be better spent protecting the animals' natural habitats. Which do you think is more important, and why?

Ana: Protecting habitats is more important. If the forests and wetlands disappear, there will be nowhere to return the animals bred in zoos.

David: Zoos are necessary because some species are so rare that they could disappear before their habitats are protected. Breeding programs buy time.
sets.note: 具体例（森・海など）を1つ入れると展開点が上がる。

sets.prompt:
Your professor is teaching a class on education. Write a post responding to the professor's question.

Professor: Some universities now require all students to take at least one course outside their major, such as an art course for engineering students. Do you think this kind of requirement is valuable? Why or why not?

Chris: Yes. Taking a course in a different field helps students think creatively and solve problems in new ways.

Yuna: I am not sure. University is expensive, and students should be free to spend their time on courses that prepare them for their careers.
sets.note: 自分の経験を短く1つ入れると説得力が出る。

sets.prompt:
Your professor is teaching a class on art. Write a post responding to the professor's question.

Professor: Many museums now offer virtual tours online, where people can view artworks from home. Do you think virtual tours can replace visiting a museum in person? Why or why not?

Liam: Virtual tours are great because anyone can see famous works without traveling. For many people, this is the only way to see them.

Nora: Seeing a painting online is not the same. The size, texture, and atmosphere of a real museum cannot be shown on a screen.
sets.note: 「完全には置き換えられない、ただし…」のような条件付きの立場もよい。

sets.prompt:
Your professor is teaching a class on sociology. Write a post responding to the professor's question.

Professor: More companies are allowing employees to work from home several days a week. Some say this improves workers' lives; others worry that it weakens teamwork. In your opinion, what is the biggest effect of working from home, and why?

Paulo: The biggest effect is more free time. Without a long commute, people can exercise, cook, and spend time with family.

Hana: I think the biggest effect is on young employees. They miss the chance to learn by watching experienced colleagues in the office.
sets.note: 「一番大きい影響」を1つに絞り、理由と例で支える。

sets.prompt:
Your professor is teaching a class on environmental science. Write a post responding to the professor's question.

Professor: To reduce plastic waste, governments can either ban certain plastic products or encourage companies to develop better recycling systems. Which approach do you think is more effective? Why?

Isabel: Bans are more effective. Recycling has existed for decades, yet most plastic still ends up in landfills or the ocean.

Marcus: Bans can create new problems, such as replacing plastic with materials that use more energy. Improving recycling solves the problem without these side effects.
sets.note: どちらかを選び、相手の意見への反論を1文入れると構成がよくなる。

Repeat the sentence exactly.
